opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it started from a kind of dissatisfaction. When I began my PhD at MIT, so much of NLP treated language as text alone: you'd train models on large corpora, predict the next word or a label, and measure success on benchmarks. That was powerful, but it always felt like something was missing. Humans don't learn language just by reading. We learn it by doing things in the world, by connecting words to actions, objects, and outcomes.

So I got really interested in the question of meaning. What does it actually mean for a system to *understand* an instruction? One answer that appealed to me was that understanding shows up in behavior. If I tell an agent "go pick up the key and open the door," and it can actually do that in an environment it hasn't seen before, that's a much more concrete signal of understanding than matching some annotated label.

That led me toward reinforcement learning combined with language. We worked on things like text-based games, where an agent has to read descriptions of its surroundings and decide what to do, with only sparse rewards telling it whether it's succeeding. We also looked at whether agents could use text, like a manual describing how objects in an environment behave, to transfer knowledge to new settings faster. The idea was that language could be a huge shortcut for learning. Instead of an agent discovering everything through trial and error, it could read about the world and get a head start, the same way people do.

Working with Regina Barzilay was a big part of it too. She really encouraged going after problems that were a bit unconventional and didn't fit neatly into existing benchmarks. And looking back, a lot of those threads, like learning from interaction, using language as an interface for acting, and building agents rather than just classifiers, have come back in a big way now that we have these large language models acting as agents. In some sense it feels like the field has circled back to the questions that excited me back then, just with far more capable tools.

r001.rationale: The response says Narasimhan pursued reinforcement learning combined with language, training agents to act on language-based instructions and treating successful behavior as evidence of understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it started with a frustration more than a plan. When I got to MIT and started working with Regina Barzilay, the dominant paradigm in NLP was that you'd take a big pile of text, learn statistics over it, and hope the patterns you picked up corresponded to something meaningful. And it worked, to a degree, but there was this nagging question underneath it: what does the model actually know about the words it's manipulating? If it says "the cup is on the table," there's no cup and no table anywhere in the system. It's just symbols predicting other symbols.

That bothered me. Language, for humans, isn't a closed system. We learn what "heavy" means by lifting things, what "left" means by turning. The meaning comes from the connection to the world and to action. So the question I kept coming back to was: can we get a machine to acquire language in a way that's tied to something it can do, or perceive, or get feedback on?

The concrete thing that pulled me in was games, actually. We started working on text-based adventure games, these old interactive fiction environments where everything the agent sees is a paragraph of text and everything it does is a typed command. What I loved about that setup was that it forced the issue. The agent couldn't succeed by just modeling text statistics. It had to read "there is a locked door to the north" and translate that into a plan, and if it misunderstood, it would get stuck, and that failure signal would come back as reward. Suddenly language understanding had a consequence.

And the flip side was just as interesting. We also looked at the reverse direction, where you have a task you want to solve, say a planning problem or a game you don't know the rules of, and there's a manual sitting next to it written in English. Can an agent read the manual and actually play better? That felt like such a natural thing for humans to do and such an alien thing for machines at the time.

So I'd say what drew me in was the sense that grounding was where the real test of understanding lived. It's easy to look fluent. It's much harder to be right when the world pushes back. And in hindsight, a lot of what I've done since, including the agent work, is really still chasing that same question, just with much more capable models underneath.

r001.rationale: The response describes an agent learning to connect language with actions in text-based games, where mistakes produce a reward signal. This communicates reinforcement learning as a way to ground and teach language understanding.

astra-6.text:
What drew me to grounding was the question of how language connects to the world. We learn words through what we see, what we do, and the consequences of our actions. I was interested in whether we could build systems that learned some of those connections, rather than learning only from text.

That also brought language and decision-making together for me. If an agent reads an instruction, can it use that instruction to act? And can the feedback from its actions help it understand the language better? That felt like a rich direction to explore during my PhD.

r001.rationale: The response connects language understanding with acting and says action feedback could improve language understanding, but it does not identify reinforcement learning as the method used to teach systems.

sol-6.1.text:
What drew me to it was the connection between language and acting in the world. We learn language alongside what we see and do, and I was interested in whether we could give machines some of that connection, rather than treating language purely as text.

During my PhD, I explored that through text-based games. An agent gets a description of its surroundings and has to choose actions to make progress. So understanding language has a consequence: it changes what the agent does and whether it succeeds. That gave us a way to study language understanding and learning to act together.

r001.rationale: The response describes language-grounding through text-based games where agents choose actions, but it does not mention reinforcement learning or clearly say that RL teaches systems to understand language.
